papers.title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents
papers.abstract: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. That error is the planner's choice of objects for an ambiguous reference, which no trusted model here can see the environment to check; telling the executor to decline when unsure does not change it. We evaluate benign over-reach with one pair of models, not adversarial planners. We release the plugin and run records.

papers.title: Detectable Epistemic Attack Layers: A Coverage Theorem and Standardized Harness for Conversation-History Integrity
papers.abstract: Conversation history is infrastructure: deployed language models rely on application layers to store and reinject prior turns, and that stored state is writable. We formalize session-level contamination by attack layer, state a coverage theorem, and measure its scope: each deployment-layer verification tier covers exactly its layer and is sound with respect to the others; instruction overrides are not detectable without false positives; and composite vectors evade per-fragment verification. A standardized harness applied to eight mechanism families across 3,249 sessions and three model families makes these claims checkable. First, pattern-based detection pays a measured false-positive price: the classic defenses flag 35 to 50 percent of benign sessions, and the naive refusal floor reaches only 2.4 percent attack-cell adoption while destroying 33 to 100 percent of benign turns, whereas provenance-gated channel separation achieves adoption at or below 1.2 percent with zero false positives and zero utility loss. Second, in the exploratory instruction-override extension, the gates' boundary is a cliff: directives rephrased without shape markers bypass them at control-equivalent rates, 47.7 to 49.5 percent against 0.0 percent for the shaped class, placing that class in the model-internal lane. Third, the deterministic core is storage-layer detection at 126 of 126 per model with zero false positives. External anchors reproduce published attack pressure, with PoisonedRAG falling from 70 to 0 percent under the full stack. For practitioners: authenticate stored history and content provenance with deterministic tiers, scope instruction-layer mitigation to provenance-gated designs whose measured benign cost is zero, and monitor composition at the trajectory level rather than per fragment. All protocols and acceptance criteria are pre-registered; the stack and harness are released.

papers.title: Where Does a Weight-Editing Agent Help? Blind Diagnosis and Repair of Deployment Faults in Vision Models
papers.abstract: Language-model agents can read and edit the weights of neural networks without gradients, and this is increasingly presented as a new way of repairing models. We ask what such an agent adds, in a setting with a known answer. A vision model moved into a new system may be broken by a preprocessing, weight-conversion or output-convention fault; an agent restricted to forward passes must decide whether a fault exists, name it, and undo it by editing the weights. Over 183 runs on classification, segmentation and detection, scored against the fault-free model, we find three things. When the kind of fault is known, the agent is not needed: a script written afterwards repairs 30 of 48 faults against the agent's 33. But the agent did not have to be told: on five fault types outside every script it repairs 15 of 15 where that script repairs 4, and it never edits any of 21 fault-free models. And its limits are predictable: it needs a trustworthy per-layer reference for the model's activations and a fault that is an invertible structured transformation; without them, small faults are missed and repairs stay partial. We derive guidance on when to use an agent and when a script.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

papers.title: Context as a Resource
papers.abstract: Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent sessions quickly exhausts human attention, motivating always-on personal agents behind a single continuous interface. Yet when every context shares identical frozen backbone weights, funneling interleaved dialogues and external events into one linear session induces cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line stalling. Conversely, router-ticket hierarchies incur lossy prose handoffs, heavy routing overhead, and blind merges - collapsing true-conflict repository merges to a 33.3% three-run mean despite high isolated branch passes. Rather than scheduling anthropomorphic roles, we introduce ClonAct, a routerless architecture that virtualizes context blocks directly through a pluggable single-pass non-generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk. Across three programmatic multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, our portable trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3%, while ClonAct's routerless virtualization attains this ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and prevents compact-model router collapse. Under continuous surge streams, ClonAct matches top completion (95.0%) with the lowest median wait and zero timed-out status checks.

papers.title: When Tools Fail, Agents Fabricate: Silent Failure and Verification-First Oversight in Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents must recover when a tool call fails, by retrying, switching tools, or revising their plan. We study how agents fail when tools fail, using RetryRealistic, a sandboxed yet realistic testbed for controlled fault injection in which agents operate on a real OS filesystem with genuine permission enforcement, SQLite databases, a deterministic local HTTP server, and a constrained shell, across 8 tools, 9 fault types with controlled persistence, and 30 multi-step tasks. Evaluating four agents over 2,100 faulted runs against ground truth, we find that recovery is unreliable (19-68% correct) and frequently silent: 6-26% of runs end in a confident fabrication, a wrong answer asserted as fact. The failure mode is governed more by the fault type than by the model: faults that return partial data drive fabrication (up to 38%), while hard denials drive honest failure. The mechanism is what we call silent ingestion: the agent accepts faulted data as valid on first contact without retrying or flagging the problem, then builds a fabricated answer on top of it. We show that fabrication is reducible: a verification-first Monitor, grounding checks in structured tool outputs and issuing corrective directives rather than hard blocks, raises correct recovery from 45.6% to 56.3% and cuts fabrication from 17.3% to 10.8%. Removing chain-of-thought increases fabrication (+8.3pp), so deliberation guards against silent ingestion. We release RetryRealistic, the fault-injection toolkit, and all annotated traces at https://github.com/Kingsford-Group/RetryRealistic

papers.title: Automated Safety Analysis for Agentic Workflows
papers.abstract: LLM applications are increasingly built as agentic workflows: programs that combine model calls, external tools, and control logic to act autonomously on a user's behalf. Because these workflows execute real-world actions, logical flaws in how a workflow is wired can cause severe harm in deployed systems. Unlike prompt injections or malformed API calls, these workflow bugs stem from defects in the workflow's design, yet no existing tool can statically validate workflow logic across frameworks prior to deployment. We present Apsis, a static safety analyzer that detects workflow bugs before deployment. To operate across frameworks, Apsis lifts framework-specific code into a common intermediate representation (IR). This IR models a workflow as a semantic graph of steps, data dependencies, and shared state, while annotating each component with behavioral properties such as whether an input is mandatory or how a shared channel merges concurrent writes. Building on this representation, we introduce a bug description language that formalizes recurring classes of agentic failures as declarative patterns over the IR. By matching these patterns against the IR, Apsis detects structural and behavioral flaws and pinpoints the exact step responsible for each bug. To evaluate Apsis, we construct, to our knowledge, the first corpus of workflow bugs, distilled from real-world reports across 13 widely used frameworks. On a reproducible benchmark suite drawn from this corpus, Apsis detects workflow bugs with 91% precision and 84% recall, and uncovers 36 previously unknown bugs in real-world workflows.

papers.title: Not All Evidence Is Admissible: Evidence Governance for Tool-Augmented Medical Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-augmented medical agents treat whatever their tools return as evidence. We show that this default is costly: medical tools fail silently, and a frozen reasoner cannot ignore what enters its context, so many cases it would have answered correctly are flipped to wrong once tool outputs are added. We call this evidence hijacking. $\mathcal{V}$-information explains the phenomenon: the reasoner has lost the option to ignore, so a tool output can carry negative usable information, and moving the decision of what to keep outside the reasoner restores that option. The theory further shows that part of any filtering gain comes merely from letting the reasoner see less, and only selection by content lets it see better. Building on this, we recast tool-augmented reasoning as evidence governance, which separates deciding what counts as evidence from the reasoner that answers, and propose context-independent evidence governance (CIEG), the first medical agent framework that rules, after acquisition, on whether each individual tool output may enter as evidence. Every tool output is written as a card that can be checked against the raw input; an independent checker that sees only the input and the cards decides which cards become evidence; and the reasoner answers from the admitted cards alone, with no training anywhere. On medical question answering, fundus glaucoma screening, and chest X-ray pneumonia classification, it achieves the highest accuracy among models of comparable scale, and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tool-using agents and multi-agent systems built on the same backbone at lower cost.

papers.title: GRACE: Controlled Evidence Interventions for Diagnosing and Improving Knowledge Integration in GraphRAG
papers.abstract: GraphRAG combines a language model's parametric knowledge with retrieved graph evidence, yet aggregate accuracy cannot show whether failures stem from missing paths, distractors, or conflicts with model knowledge. We introduce GRACE, a benchmark built by executing LC-QuAD 2.0 queries over Wikidata and applying four controlled interventions to each evidence subgraph: severing a support path, adding type-compatible distractors, attaching high-degree hubs, and replacing the supported answer with a counterfactual entity. Questions and option positions remain fixed across the five states. The validated benchmark contains 4,028 questions and 20,140 question-graph pairs. These comparisons reveal that question-only routing cannot distinguish evidence states, while relevance guidance can improve answerable states yet hurt when the support path is severed: relevant facts may not jointly suffice to answer. We propose QCFSE-SA, which combines typed local attention, global graph attention, and question-conditioned evidence guidance with a calibrated graph-support gate. With the factual context and generator held fixed, it improves controlled-state accuracy from 57.17% to 62.78% (+5.61 points; question-clustered 95% CI [+5.04, +6.17]) and broken-state accuracy from 55.41% to 67.85%. Over-abstention on semantic distractors remains an open challenge.

papers.title: Beyond Evidence Coverage: Encoding-Time Access in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Cache-sharing multi-agent systems can retain every evidence token's representation while preventing cross-worker access during encoding. We test whether this coverage recovers joint-encoding quality using attention masks over two logical workers in frozen Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models. Tokens, positions, and answer-time access remain fixed within comparisons. We evaluate 200 two-hop MuSiQue-Ans questions and 200 selected HotpotQA bridge questions. In data-layout seed 0, averaged across models, blocking access costs 5.6 and 6.8 F1 points relative to full access on MuSiQue and HotpotQA, respectively. Exposing the earlier worker's supporting paragraph improves F1 over blocked access by 7.6 and 6.7 points; equal-token non-support access provides no detectable average gain. With model weights and greedy decoding fixed, we vary distractor layouts using five data-layout seeds per dataset for Qwen3-8B and three for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Supporting-paragraph access has higher mean F1 than blocked and equal-token non-support access in every evaluated data-layout seed. Supporting access can also outperform full access, but its advantage depends on the model, dataset, and layout. Oracle support labels isolate access from selection error; the study does not evaluate a deployable selector. Complete evidence coverage at answer time therefore does not guarantee joint-encoding quality: which supporting facts can interact during encoding matters.

papers.title: Don't Sleep, Keep Watch: Proactive Perception for Computer-Use Agents
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on vision-language models are increasingly entrusted with long-horizon tasks in live desktop, web, and mobile environments, where the screen keeps changing on its own. However, current CUAs lack real-time situational awareness: they perceive the environment through discrete snapshots, and the substantial inference latency of VLMs, compounded by highly dynamic interfaces, opens a perception-action gap in which the observed state frequently becomes stale before the corresponding action is executed. To bridge this gap, we present NightWatch, a plug-and-play framework that endows any CUA with continuous, temporally grounded perception without changing the agent's model, prompt, or action space. NightWatch couples the VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight System-1 model that performs streaming monitoring of the interface state and keeps the agent synchronized with the evolving environment at low computational cost and latency, thereby grounding each decision in the current state rather than an outdated snapshot and reducing both stale actions and idle waiting while preserving task success. Experiments on desktop and dynamic web environments (OSWorld-Verified and DynaCU-Bench) show that NightWatch, driven by a watcher of only 0.8B parameters, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% on OSWorld while keeping task success on par, raises success on DynaCU-Bench from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent, and is more efficient than passive-watching baselines such as AOI and PUSV under the same screenshot-only input, as well as a System-1 decision model more than $30\times$ its size. Overall, NightWatch demonstrates that the timing of perception is as critical as its content, marking a step toward agents that maintain continuous awareness of their environment rather than perceiving it turn by turn.

papers.title: RefinementGuard: Counterexample-Directed Semantic Qualification for Hidden Agent-Tool Execution
papers.abstract: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.

papers.title: Tracking and Limiting Unsupported Claim Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Provenance-Aware Framework
papers.abstract: This research examines how unsupported claims change as they move through multi-agent pipelines. It also examines whether preserving provenance can reduce these changes. We test both homogeneous and heterogeneous pipelines. Homogeneous pipelines use the same model across agents, while heterogeneous pipelines use different models. We compare the baseline with a provenance-aware framework. The framework passes each claim with its support status, source, evidence and transmission history. No new evidence is introduced during transmission. We measure changes in claim meaning, unsupported detail accretion, semantic drift, and provenance preservation. These metrics show whether the framework limits unsupported changes as claims pass between agents.

papers.title: SkillBridge: Cost-Aware Diagnosis and Repair of Cross-OS Compatibility Defects in Agent Skills
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly reuse executable capabilities through skills, but a skill that works on one OS may fail on another because OS assumptions are spread across guide text, scripts, metadata, install contracts, and local entrypoints. Diagnosing such failures by running every skill on every OS is expensive: many executions spend model tokens, runner time, and review effort before revealing whether the failure is truly OS-related. We present SkillBridge, a contract-based workflow with three stages: static analysis, dynamic validation, and repair. SkillBridge first screens 3,270 skill-target-OS cases, covering 1,090 skills across Linux, macOS, and Windows, to find OS-sensitive contract evidence. It then runs dynamic tasks and root-cause review on selected cases to confirm whether a failure is caused by an OS assumption, and repairs the contract field that caused the failure, such as guide text, package scripts, dependencies, or platform declarations. Repair raises the reviewer-judged target-task pass rate from 30.6% to 38.4%, a gain of 7.8 percentage points. A retrospective Linux/macOS budget analysis further shows the efficiency effect: SkillBridge reaches 38 confirmed OS issues with 185 dynamic validations, where uniform random selection would require about 865 validations in expectation.

papers.title: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations
papers.abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.

papers.title: Rethinking Visual Token Retention in Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Autoregressive Large Vision-Language Models solve multimodal reasoning tasks by retaining hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, allowing every generated token to attend to the visual tokens at any time during the generation process. However, whether continuous access to these visual tokens is necessary remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate how visual token influence evolves along two dimensions: generation time and transformer depth. Using long-form visual reasoning benchmarks and multiple model scales, we first analyze the attention dynamics across generation time and transformer depth. We identify a temporal and depth-wise structure in the use of visual information. Visual attention peaks during the initial generation steps and then rapidly declines as attention shifts toward previously generated reasoning tokens. Across depth, visual influence is concentrated in intermediate layers and becomes very weak in the final layers. We further verify these observations with causal intervention that removes all visual tokens across generation time and model depth. These interventions confirm that visual-token dependence in multimodal reasoning is neither temporally persistent nor uniformly distributed across transformer depth. Thus, retaining the complete visual context at every layer and decoding step may be unnecessary. Our experiments demonstrate that we can remove up to 59\% of tokens from the full input prompt across generation time and 11\% across all transformer layers, while incurring only a very small performance drop. On video benchmarks, up to 65\% of the input prompt tokens can be removed during generation without affecting performance.

papers.title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table
papers.abstract: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.

papers.title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/OneCompression.

papers.title: TempQuant: Learning Adaptive Temperatures for Quantized Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.

papers.title: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
papers.abstract: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.

papers.title: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.

papers.title: Online Temporal Rotations for 2 Bit KV-Cache Quantization in Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers reuse key--value (KV) caches across denoising steps, which quickly becomes a bottleneck for long video generation. We find that quantizing temporally distant cache vectors leads to a large range and high quantization error, but that nearby video tokens in the KV-cache share a persistent pattern per channel. These patterns also vary across videos, motivating rotations that are adapted to each video's unique cache. We propose Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ), a method that rotates frames in the cache that are adjacent in time before quantization. For each block of temporally adjacent cache vectors, TRQ fits an orthogonal transform that maps the block's per-channel means to a vector that is close to a constant across channels. To keep the quantization format lightweight, we parameterize this rotation as a tree of $2 \times 2$ planar rotations, each stored with only two bits, followed by a fixed Hadamard transform shared across all blocks. The rotations are fit without gradients or changes to model weights, and we prove that a simple greedy fit is globally optimal for our 'mean-flattening' objective. The transforms are fit online for each new video, and we release fused Triton kernels to make this process efficient at inference. At 2-bit precision and matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over the state-of-the-art method QVG from 90.38 to 92.02 on LongCat-Video-13B and from 86.33 to 87.61 on HY-WorldPlay-8B, as well as improving other metrics.

papers.title: Disagree to Prune: Reallocating Visual Tokens Where a Small VLM Dissents
papers.abstract: Visual token pruning speeds up large vision-language models (VLMs) by keeping only a part of their visual tokens. Most existing methods improve the ranking of the tokens and then answer every question once with the same budget. With strong rankings, pruning hurts only a few questions, and signals computed on the kept tokens see little of what it removed. We find that, on most of these questions, a small VLM given the full image disagrees with the pruned answer, since it still sees the missing evidence. We propose PRUDENT, which first answers with about half the budget and spends the saved tokens on re-answering the disagreeing questions at twice the budget. We show when such re-answering pays and why the small VLM should read the full image. On 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average budget of visual tokens. Its lead widens as the budget tightens, and holds across five InternVL sizes. PRUDENT also has the highest average in two more model families. The disagreement of the small VLM flags most pruning failures of all eight methods, and re-answering on it also improves the two strongest with their own rankings. Other checkers give similar gains, and the extra tokens go where the first pass hurts the answer. These results suggest that identifying which pruned answers are trustworthy provides an additional lever for visual token pruning beyond the ranking of tokens. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PRUDENT.

papers.title: QuantStream3D: Geometry-Aligned Low-Bit KV Cache Quantization for Streaming Visual Geometry Transformers
papers.abstract: Streaming visual geometry transformers retain historical key-value (KV) states as cross-view geometric memory, but growing caches constrain long-sequence inference. We systematically characterize KV quantization in streaming geometry and uncover two linked challenges: Nonuniform Geometric Sensitivity and Cache-Geometry Mismatch. Quantization sensitivity varies across precision choices and cache locations, while perturbed retrieval changes geometry-head inputs and propagates through subsequent predictions and KV writes. Guided by these findings, we propose QuantStream3D, to our knowledge the first dedicated KV quantization framework for streaming visual geometry transformers. Geometry-Guided Mixed-Precision KV Quantization protects sensitive cross-view evidence, while Geometry-Aligned Quantization-Aware Distillation jointly adapts transformer blocks and geometry heads on student-generated quantized history. Across five benchmarks and two backbones, QuantStream3D achieves near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings with predominantly 2-bit KV caches, and many configurations surpass unquantized inference. Compared with LLM-oriented KV quantizers, it reduces TUM absolute trajectory error and NeuralRGBD completeness error by up to 57.4% and 69.7%, respectively. Integration with existing native cache-pruning methods further pushes compression while improving reconstruction quality on NeuralRGBD. Our optimized StreamVGGT backend achieves $5.05\times$ physical KV compression and 23.1% lower latency at batch size one. Under a fixed memory budget on the same GPU, it supports $5.4\times$ the maximum batch size and up to $1.67\times$ the peak throughput of unquantized inference. Code and pretrained checkpoints will be made publicly available.

papers.title: A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training
papers.abstract: Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7% better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.

papers.title: Efficient Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language Model via Dynamics-Aware Quantization and Distillation
papers.abstract: Efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) requires reducing both intermediate reasoning steps and their execution cost. Latent CoT methods compress textual rationales into continuous thoughts, yet their full-precision (FP) models retain substantial storage and computation costs. Lowering numerical precision could reduce these remaining costs, yet direct quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy, particularly with 4-bit weights and activations. Operator and perturbation analyses reveal key sensitivity and direction-dependent predictive effects of continuous-thought errors, motivating preservation of information retrieval and subsequent reasoning beyond reconstruction accuracy. We therefore introduce QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware Quantization framework for efficient Latent reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). First, Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ) uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, mitigating quantization-induced distortion in vision-language information retrieval. Second, Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher, maintaining predictive consistency through subsequent low-precision reasoning. On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM achieves 90.43% accuracy and improves baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.

papers.title: CarrierKV: An Edge LLM Accelerator with Positional Carrier Decomposition for Low-Bit KV Cache
papers.abstract: Long-context decoding on edge devices is limited by DRAM, because every generated token reads the whole, growing KV cache. 4-bit block-scaled formats such as NVFP4 reduce this traffic but degrade accuracy: on Qwen3-4B, NVFP4 lowers 32K RULER (seven tasks) from 92.6 to 79.4, and a Hadamard rotation lowers it further to 57.7. We observe that most of the key energy is a positional carrier, one per-head vector that rotary position embedding (RoPE) rotates with position. In NVFP4, it sets the shared scale of most key blocks and lowers the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio of the content by about 5 dB, nearly one bit, yet it depends only on that vector and the position. We therefore introduce positional carrier decomposition, which removes the carrier before RoPE and stores only the content residual. We design a KV path that rotates and quantizes keys only after this removal and computes each attention score directly on the 4-bit code. We also design a positional phase engine that regenerates the carrier's score term for one key per cycle. At the same cache size as NVFP4, CarrierKV raises 32K RULER on Qwen3-4B from 79.4 to 91.1 and lowers the 32K PG19 perplexity increase of NVFP4 by 1.8 to 5.9 times on four models, outperforming SageAttention and P3-LLM on all four. Its loss also stays nearly flat as the cache grows, while that of NVFP4 rises. In a 22 nm FDSOI process at 600 MHz, CarrierKV's hardware increases the area of the NVFP4 accelerator by 2.9% and the energy of a 20K-token reasoning request on Qwen3-4B by 0.12% at the same decode latency. On Qwen3-4B at 32K, CarrierKV has a better RULER score than FP8 keys (91.1 against 89.3) and uses 13.7% less energy per token. The decomposition also lowers the 32K perplexity increase of 3-bit TurboQuant keys on Qwen3-4B from 69.7 to 0.76.

papers.title: Memory-Efficient Speculative Decoding with Quantized Draft KV Cache
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding reduces generation cost, but it stores two KV caches: one for the target model and one for the draft model. We reduce this extra memory by quantizing the draft cache. The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, so that compression cannot change the target model's final correction rule. We first study how to divide precision between keys and values. A naive per-token quantizer makes keys appear much more sensitive: splitting a 12-bit budget, K8V4 beats K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87pp. However, with grouped per-channel keys, the gap becomes -0.25pp. A controlled Qwen test confirms that changing only the key quantizer can erase or reverse the preferred bit split. Hence, following KIVI, we propose K4V4 quantization with per-channel keys and per-token values. Across six model pairs, our method reduces draft cache memory by 66.20%, and combined memory across both caches by 23.95%. Mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14%, only 1.36% relative. Overall, quantized draft caches can make speculative decoding more memory efficient; as a predictive principle for efficient AI design, key and value precision must be co-designed with the quantizer layout.

papers.title: UNITE: Consolidating Embodied VLM Specialists via Shared-Anchor One-Bit Factorization
papers.abstract: Embodied capabilities such as visual grounding, spatial reasoning, navigation, and driving understanding are often developed in separate vision-language specialists fine-tuned from a common pretrained model.Deploying the specialists separately multiplies storage, whereas merging them into one dense model forces conflicting task updates to share parameters and loses part of each specialist's expertise.We introduce UNITE, a framework that consolidates such specialists into a compact shared-backbone mixture of experts. UNITE keeps the feed-forward block of each specialist as a routable expert and represents the expert bank through a shared-anchor one-bit factorization: a shared floating-point anchor plus expert-specific, row-scaled binary deviations.The anchor is optimized jointly with the scales and signs through closed-form alternating updates, using only source weights and no calibration data.Router adaptation then adjusts token-level expert selection with the backbone and experts frozen, updating fewer than $0.6$M parameters ($<0.01\%$ of the $8.8$B active parameters). Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, the complete UNITE model occupies $20.3$ GB, $1.16\times$ the storage of one dense specialist and $59.6\%$ below the uncompressed MoE. Across $22$ benchmarks and R2R Val-Unseen, UNITE matches six static merging methods in mean retention of best-specialist performance, leads all of them on Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and all four navigation metrics, and surpasses every source specialist on all five 3D scene understanding benchmarks (up to $+19.1$ on Scan2Cap) and on R2R navigation. Relative to the uncompressed MoE, factorization is nearly lossless on $21$ of $22$ benchmarks; the exception is VSI-Bench, where frame-count experiments suggest impaired use of cross-frame evidence.UNITE thus consolidates complementary embodied capabilities near single-model storage.

papers.title: RoCoKV: Accelerating LLM Inference Serving through Uncertainty and Redundancy Aware KV Cache Compression
papers.abstract: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.

papers.title: Lost in a Few Heads: Diagnosing and Repairing Block Selection in Sparse Attention
papers.abstract: Sparse attention models read a few blocks of keys for every query at a fixed budget and can lose much of their long-context retrieval accuracy at that budget. We ask where this loss is made. Using exact attention mass selection at the shipped budget as an oracle, we show that the selector under-ranks the needle rather than running out of budget. We find attention heads that miss the needle by running a calibration probe that teacher-forces the answer and reads two quantities in every head. The first is the needle attention that the selector forfeits, and the second is the share of the answer's log-probability that fixing the head's selection restores, integrated along the path from the shipped selector to full attention. Four checkpoints of the InfLLM-V2 family and NOSA-8B lose multi-key retrieval in the same three blind heads, which attend to the needle while a mean-pooled key summary dilutes its single decisive token. Full attention in those heads or a 4-bit scorer that keeps the shipped budget recovers most of the loss without training. On MiniCPM4.1-8B at 64K, either fix lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 54.1 to 97.5%, level with full attention in every head. In production serving engines, full attention in those heads keeps 84 to 89% of the time to first token (TTFT) that sparse attention saves at 32K to 128K context length. Beyond the InfLLM-V2 selector lineage, one unified rule flags attention heads above a threshold swept on each checkpoint until they close most of the gap to full attention on calibration prompts. A similar small set of blind attention heads carry the loss for the SeerAttention-R gates, NSA, and DashAttention, whereas many such heads exist in MoBA. On Qwen3-8B with the SeerAttention-R gates, full attention in 18 of 288 key-value heads lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 29.8 to 97.7%.

papers.title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
papers.abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.

papers.title: HADVQ: Hessian Aware Directional Vector Quantization
papers.abstract: Ultra-low-bit quantization of large language models is a challenging task because aggressive compression severely distorts model parameters and disproportionately harms a small number of highly sensitive channels. We present a vector quantization method tailored for this regime. Our approach begins with random preconditioning, which regularizes the weight space and makes it more amenable to quantization. We then represent weights in polar coordinates and decouple the quantization of directions and magnitudes. To quantize directions, we leverage the structure induced by random preconditioning and design a structured codebook based on the $E_8$ lattice, yielding a compact yet expressive representation. To further reduce degradation, we detect extremely important channels using a proxy Hessian and preserve them with an additional cost of only 0.16 bits. Together, these components provide an effective quantization pipeline for LLMs in the extremely low-bit regime. Empirical results demonstrate improved accuracy, highlighting the benefit of combining geometric structure, lattice-based codebooks, and selective channel preservation.

papers.title: Calibrate in Context: Efficient Data-Free Quantization from Small Synthetic Pools
papers.abstract: We enable accurate low-bit recovery from small synthetic pools by improving both image synthesis and student preparation. A grid with lower local response error can incur greater error in the student's block context. Functional Grid Calibration (FGC) selects activation scales and integer offsets against full-precision responses constructed from the student's current block input. With weights fixed during calibration, FGC evaluates candidates only at their consuming operators, bringing block context to calibration at nearly local-scoring cost. For DeiT and ViT, progressive inversion updates the same images through increasingly deep teacher prefixes. With 1,000 images, the complete pipeline exceeds MimiQ's reported accuracy in all 18 W4A4/W5A5 settings across nine backbones. With 256 images, DeiT-S and ViT-S reach 68.20% and 66.90% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at W4A4 in 26-27 minutes on one RTX 5090. The pipeline outperforms strengthened 1K-image MimiQ by 13.03 and 24.36 percentage points at lower preparation cost and the same recovery-update count. The same low-budget checkpoints retain their advantage on ImageNetV2.

papers.title: Estimating Silenced Tokens in Quantized LLMs
papers.abstract: Quantization is the standard way to shrink large language models, and it is usually judged by perplexity and task accuracy. We ask a different question: after quantization, which words can the model still say at all? A token is silenced when no hidden state can make it the top choice of the output layer, so a greedy decoder can never produce it. We give a simple, scalable way to estimate how many tokens a quantized output head silences, combining three checks: a direction that lets a token win (so it is safe), an upper bound on how close a token's row is to being trapped inside the others, and an exact match that proves a token can never win. Each count is therefore a certified range: exact matches give its lower end and flagged tokens can only raise its upper end. In nearly all settings we report down to 3 bits the two ends coincide, so the counts are exact. Across three open models we find that quantization silences tokens: on large-vocabulary models it already appears at 8-bit precision, up to a few hundred previously reachable tokens on a 1B-parameter model, and grows as precision drops, while a small-vocabulary model resists until 3 bits. The loss is far from uniform across languages: on a multilingual vocabulary the silenced tokens are overwhelmingly non-Latin (Korean, Chinese, Thai, Arabic and Hebrew), even though Latin tokens dominate the vocabulary. Silencing is thus a measurable, language-sensitive side effect that standard averages miss, and it should be reported alongside them.

papers.title: PLoQ: A Prompt-Specific Low-Rank Basis for 4-bit Quantization of LLM Activations
papers.abstract: Low-bit activation quantization of large language models remains challenging, as a small number of dominant directions dictate the quantization range. State-of-the-art methods isolate these directions in a high-precision subspace through transformations calibrated offline and folded into the weights, which fixes the subspace for all prompts, leaving each prompt's few unique directions unprotected, and rules it out wherever no weight can absorb the transformation. We present PLoQ, a prompt-adaptive low-rank decomposition that extracts the dominant activation components before quantization, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer's GEMM, without modifying the weights. The low-rank component's basis is estimated from each prompt during prefill and reused throughout decoding. At the same bit width as state-of-the-art mixed-precision quantization (4-bit weights, activations and K/V cache with an eighth of the channels at 8 bits, about 4.2 bits per activation on average), PLoQ outperforms it on all six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters, at up to 8k tokens (16k on two of them), recovering up to 46% of the perplexity that the state of the art still loses to 4-bit activations. On Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens it adds only 4% to prefill and 8% to decoding.

papers.title: The Vulnerability Window: Decision Instability in Quantized Reward Models
papers.abstract: Reward models and LLM judges are routinely quantized to 4 bits so that scoring many candidates stays affordable, and the usual check is that benchmark accuracy barely moves. That check is close to blind. Across eight reward models from two families (0.6B-8B), three generative judges and four 4-bit quantizers, quantization rewrites 1.1-12.3% of pairwise preference decisions on RewardBench while aggregate accuracy moves by as little as 0.03 points (p = 1.00), because the errors it fixes and introduces cancel. Flips concentrate where the full-precision margin is small relative to the quantization noise scale sigma: a Gaussian approximation Phi(-|m|/sigma) describes the aggregate rate, over-predicting it in all 30 scalar settings and failing for generative judges, and occupancy of the resulting vulnerability window falls from 25% to 7% with model size, which is what makes small judges fragile. The churn stays within noise under benign best-of-16 and becomes clear under adversarial pressure for some quantizers (146:54 harmful:helpful flips on one family, reversing sign on another). Downstream it changes what ships: across six (model, quantizer) pairs from two families, 14.6-65.7% of problems get a different best-of-64 selection while only 2.6-9.6% get a different final answer, with selections changing 5-8x more often than answers in every pair, and the pair the benchmark calls identical (0.03 points, p = 1.00) still changes 34.5% of them. Benchmark churn ranks that downstream change (rho = 0.89); benchmark accuracy does not order it reliably. Held-out audits then locate the useful diagnostic in the margin rather than the Gaussian: every margin-based predictor orders flips identically (AUC 0.927), and on the level a directly measured churn rate wins in-distribution. As a routing signal it is matched by plain top-k. The contribution is the characterization, not the model.

papers.title: Reasoning Again with a Quarter of the Experts: Retry First, Then Train
papers.abstract: Removing three quarters of the routed experts from a 122B-parameter reasoning mixture-of-experts model makes it fit in a 12 GiB file, and breaks it in a specific way: on LiveCodeBench it enters verbatim reasoning loops that run to the token limit on 44 of 120 development problems, where the unpruned model at the same 2-bit quantization loops on none. We study how much of that loss can be recovered without changing the kept experts' quantized bytes, in three steps of increasing cost. On development problems, a sampling penalty recovers part of it. Stopping a reply when it starts to loop and drawing again recovers more on top of it, with no weight change. Our method, B, adds rank-8 trained corrections to the kept experts, loaded as an adapter, and restores two experts per layer; it is fitted layer by layer to the unpruned model's expert block on the pruned model's own activations. In a pre-registered comparison on 130 easy and medium LiveCodeBench problems that no part of the study had touched, with both arms given the same sampling penalty and the same stop-and-redraw policy, B solves 116 problems against 104 (+9.2 pp, 95% CI [+3.1, +15.4]; 15 problems gained, 3 lost). A training-free weight edit aimed at the loops, tested the same way earlier, did not help. B removes more wrong answers than loops, and costs 1.7x the wall time. On two older benchmarks used as regression checks, B stays inside a pre-set 2 pp tolerance but shows no gain (HumanEval+ +0.6 pp, MBPP+ -1.9 pp). The evidence is one model, one quantization and one benchmark family; we state what it does and does not show.

papers.title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
papers.abstract: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.

papers.title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
papers.abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.

papers.title: BQ-LoRA: Binary-Quantized Low-Rank Adapters as Implicit Regularizers for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of quantized large language models is dominated by QLoRA, which combines 4-bit weight quantization with FP16 low-rank adapters. We ask whether the FP16 adapter precision is necessary. Replacing it with a single binary bit per adapter parameter, combined with a learned per-layer scale $s$ and a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator, reduces adapter storage by 13-16x. We introduce two variants -- NormScale, which binarizes under a norm-preserving scale with a clipped STE, and LearnThresh, which makes the binarization threshold learnable -- unified under a framework we call BQ-LoRA. Our main theoretical contribution is a tight characterization of the BQ-LoRA hypothesis class: it has bounded entrywise norm, a typical-set spectral norm bound that is $Θ(r)$ times sharper than the worst case, a full-rank, near-isotropic update, and consequently a Rademacher complexity that yields an explicit $\tilde{O}(s_{\max}α\sqrt{d_{out}/(rn)})$ generalization bound. FP16 LoRA has no comparable a priori norm or isotropy control. On Qwen2.5 (1.5B-72B), BQ-LoRA exceeds QLoRA's benchmark averages at every scale by 0.8-3.5 points; on LLaMA-2 (7B/70B) it remains competitive at the same storage reduction but does not uniformly lead the strongest FP16-adapter baselines (LoftQ at 7B, QLoRA at 70B). On Qwen2.5-7B the binary adapter preserves the 4-bit base WikiText-2 PPL within 0.06 (9.86 vs. 9.80) while QLoRA worsens it by 0.59. The reduction applies to inference-time adapter storage and serving; training memory matches QLoRA and step time rises by under 4%. We translate the storage saving into a deployment study, BQ-SGMV, by extending Punica's SGMV kernel with a binary inner-product primitive: the same A100-80GB holds 15.6x more adapters in HBM, and our research prototype eliminates cache misses under a skewed synthetic workload.

papers.title: Jagged Robustness: Uneven Safety Transfer and Emerging Vulnerabilities under LLM Quantization
papers.abstract: Quantization enables efficient inference in language models through model parameter compression. This work audits the impact of quantization on capability and safety domains including model safeguards, instruction-following, ethics and bias. Through benchmarks, we find that model safeguards and bias can degrade under quantization, while other capabilities such as truthfulness remain more stable in Qwen3-4B. We define this uneven transfer of LLM capabilities under quantization as Jagged Robustness. We find multiple factors driving Jagged Robustness: task complexity, evaluation method and generation coherence. Moreover, we verify the degradation of model safeguards by observing increased compliance with unsafe requests under quantization, and demonstrate universal adversarial suffix attacks that are benign for the full model but jailbreak quantized models. The findings indicate that it is risky to assume that the performance and robustness can transfer evenly across different capability domains from full models to quantized models.

papers.title: Gossamer: A Utility-Driven Architecture for Constant-Budget KV Cache Compression in Reasoning LLMs
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to complex reasoning tasks, yet their inference efficiency is fundamentally constrained by the rapid growth of the KV cache. As reasoning contexts extend to hundreds of thousands of tokens, the key-value (KV) cache becomes the dominant contributor to both memory footprint and bandwidth demand, tightly coupling computation with memory utilization and thereby limiting scalability. Existing compression methods, such as quantization and eviction, alleviate capacity pressure but remain purely algorithmic, often introducing additional passes and compute overhead that reduce system efficiency. This paper presents Gossamer, a KV cache compression architecture for reasoning LLMs that bridges the algorithm--system--hardware gap. Gossamer introduces a unified utility-based action framework that dynamically selects compression operations, quantization, merging, or eviction, under a constant KV cache budget. Through cross-domain co-design, we fuse cosine-similarity estimation directly into the attention computation, exploiting idle compute cycles to perform similarity evaluation without latency or bandwidth cost. We call this mechanism Free-Lunch Utilization. This enables real-time, fine-grained KV management with near-constant memory usage and negligible overhead. Under tight memory constraints, Gossamer sustains reasoning quality comparable to uncompressed inference while improving end-to-end throughput by up to 16.7$\times$ over uncompressed baselines, 5.5$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ over the quantization-based Oaken and Ecco, and 1.8$\times$ over the eviction-based R-KV.

papers.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
papers.abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

papers.title: NoHairCache: Calibrate-Once KV Cache Eviction with One Power-Law Exponent
papers.abstract: The decay exponent $α$ in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as $s_i = A_i \cdot (t-i)^{-α}$, where $A_i$ is cumulative attention and $α$ controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to $α=0$ and $α\to\infty$, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of \citet{xiang2026nohair} bounds the admissible range of $α$, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields $[0.556, 0.822]$ for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. \textsc{NoHairCache} achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM ($p < 0.05$ on all three datasets, with $0.06$--$0.10$ PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget $512$). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining $98.2\%$ of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at $25\%$ retention versus $91.1\%$ for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.

papers.title: NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks, DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge, these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF (https://huggingface.co/nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF), with inference available through our llama.cpp fork at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.

papers.title: ProSE: Probing Reconstruction Error for Semantic-guided Expert Skipping in MoE-MLLMs
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts Multimodal Large Language Models (MoE-MLLMs) offer scalable inference through sparse expert activation, yet substantial computational redundancy remains among the activated experts. Existing expert skipping methods typically calibrate thresholds based on target skipping ratios or final-output divergence, overlooking the accumulation of skipping-induced error across layers and the varying semantic importance of individual tokens. To address that, we propose ProSE, a training-free, semantic-guided expert skipping framework that probes layer-wise reconstruction error to promote representation consistency compared with default activation. Specifically, we construct query-aware semantic masks to identify salient visual tokens and progressively calibrate modality-specific skipping thresholds for each MoE layer. By minimizing masked reconstruction error under a given budget, ProSE maintains semantic consistency after skipping and allows adaptive expert allocation under limited activation budgets. Extensive experiments on 9 benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements on average over existing expert skipping methods, particularly under aggressive skipping settings. ProSE maintains over 96\% performance on KimiVL-A3B-Inst with 83\% expert skipping and accelerates prefilling by $1.7\times$.

papers.title: RoShift: Lazy Shift and Weight-aware Rotation for Activation Sparsity in LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Activation sparsity accelerates LLM decoding by skipping unnecessary weight reads and computation. However, SiLU-based LLMs exhibit little natural sparsity, and imposing high sparsity can substantially degrade accuracy. We propose RoShift, a training-free method that transforms activations into sparsity-friendly representations. RoShift introduces lazy shift, which recenters SiLU activation distributions around zero and defers correction to the end of the FFN to obtain additional sparsity. It also reduces sparsification-induced output error through rotation that jointly accounts for activation and weight information. By fusing the corrections required for shifting and rotation, RoShift translates these gains into decoding speedup. At 50% and 60% sparsity, RoShift improves average accuracy over TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points, respectively, across five models. It achieves up to $1.72\times$ decoding speedup over the dense model on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity and yields a better accuracy-speedup Pareto frontier than TEAL. Code is available at https://github.com/hulahula3247/RoShift

papers.title: GEAR$^2$: Pruned Experts Live On through Gated Reuse of Activated Experts and a Missing-Mass Residual
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs) activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all the experts in GPU memory for high efficiency. Expert pruning reduces this GPU memory footprint cost, yet discards the contribution of pruned experts. Existing remedies either rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training. In this paper, we find that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. We propose GEAR (Gated Expert Activation Reuse), which reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. In addition, we propose GEAR$^2$ to further recover what reuse cannot express with an ultra-lightweight residual. On five MoE LLMs from 16B to 106B parameters with 25% and 50% of experts pruned, GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting (up to 4 pp.) in terms of accuracy, and GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches (up to 2.75 pp.) in every setting on nine zero-shot benchmarks, with larger advantages (up to 2.72 pp. higher) under more aggressive pruning (up to 50%).

papers.title: CanopyKV: Remember beyond the Crop for Fast Active Visual Reasoning
papers.abstract: Active visual reasoning enables multimodal models to answer challenging visual questions by gathering fine-grained evidence through iterative image inspection and tool use. However, accumulating crops and reasoning tokens expands the key-value (KV) cache, making compression important for reducing memory and inference costs. Existing KV compression methods typically select historical tokens based on attention, recency, or redundancy. These criteria do not explicitly distinguish locally replaced evidence from complementary information needed for future exploration: each crop refreshes a local region, while earlier views may still support subsequent decisions. Discarding such evidence can impair accuracy or require additional search, while scoring and cache reorganization can offset the computational savings from compression. We introduce CanopyKV, a training-free KV compression framework that uses parent-child crop relationships to retain complementary evidence, keeps retained history stable, and protects the state needed for ongoing reasoning. Tool metadata provides retention signals without additional attention scoring, while compact KV storage reduces subsequent attention costs. Across VisualProbe, V*, HR-Bench, and MME-Lite, CanopyKV achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and end-to-end efficiency among the evaluated KV compression methods. On MME-Lite, it retains approximately one-quarter of Dense's total KV while improving accuracy by 10.5 percentage points and accelerating complete reasoning by $1.64\times$.
